title: Smarter insurance through human-AI collaboration
excerpt: . It’s not hard to understand why more than three-quarters ( 78% ) of insurers see customer experience (CX) as central to their growth strategy. Consider Tom who reports a car accident through his insurer’s app and uploads the requested photos. When he checks the insurer’s website for an update the next day, there’s no record of his claim. Frustrated, he calls for help, only for the claims agent to ask him for the set of documents yet again. This is a common industry challenge. 42% of insurance executives cite fragmented, multi-channel journeys as a top barrier to providing a great CX today. And 60% expect it to worsen over the next few years. A discontinuity during a claim or when taking out a new policy can quickly damage customer confidence. And it shows up as cost: repeat contacts, duplicate data entry, and rework across teams. But many leading insurers are beginning to close these gaps with AI and give their frontline staff the context they need to provide better experiences. Remove friction, not the human touch. AI can make the moments that matter feel simpler. For example, at the first notice of loss (FNOL), AI can capture the essential details and ensure that all information is accurate and complete. In service and renewals, AI assistants can answer routine questions quickly and help customers with many tasks without waiting in a queue. Over half ( 53% ) of insurers say they’re already using AI for customer service, chatbots, messaging, and self-service portals. These interactions are concentrated at the FNOL and claims-intake stage, where automation lowers cost per contact and improves containment before a case reaches an adjuster. But the more important shift is not simply putting a bot in front of the customer. It’s using AI behind the scenes to give claims handlers, underwriters, agents, and contact center teams a clearer view of each case. Insurers will continue to place high value on human expertise, especially in complex claims or renewal negotiations. Our survey results show that 63% of insurance customers rank human support among their top three preferred channels. But at the same time, 59% also rank AI-integrated bots among their top three, reinforcing that a blended, human-in-the-loop model helps resolve more inquiries through self-service while maintaining effective personal support for complex cases. Many insurers are already striking this balance. For instance, The Hartford, a US-based insurance and investment company, uses AI agents to answer common questions or provide real-time claim updates. But it also uses AI to offer real-time support to agents for better first-call resolution through call summaries and sentiment analysis. Customers have a clear expectation: give us AI to simplify processes and give us frontline staff for when judgment, reassurance, and a more nuanced conversation matter to us. There’s a clear path to turn that balance from an ambition into a practical starting point. Start where friction is highest. The best place to begin is not with AI itself, but with a customer journey where friction is already visible and costly. title: Better banking needs humans and AI
excerpt: . For banking leaders, the question is no longer whether AI can improve customer experience (CX). It’s where AI should take the lead, where human judgment must remain visible, and how both can work hand in hand. You may recall that at one point merely providing digital access to customers was enough for a bank to earn its CX stripes. But today, customers place far greater value on the quality of that access. Since banking interactions often carry real financial consequences for the customer, weak CX isn’t just an inconvenience. It compounds into slower resolutions, repeat contacts, and escalations, each adding direct cost to serve in addition to the risk of reputational damage. We found that for 88% of banking executives CX is central to their growth strategy. But is delivering it consistently such a straightforward task?. Customers are not getting a unified experience. 40% of banking executives cite “fragmented journeys across multiple channels” as the greatest barrier to effective CX today, with 58% expecting it to worsen over the next three years. Fragmentation typically shows up at the handoffs customers notice most, such as when switching from a mobile app to a branch or call center mid-task or re-submitting identity documents already provided elsewhere in the institution. Each handoff adds friction for the customer and rework for the bank. And because many of these journeys touch regulated processes such as KYC (know your customer) and account changes, the cost of getting them wrong can create compliance issues and leave teams tracing records and correcting documentation. But disconnected journeys aren’t the only challenge. Banks may also be designing experiences around assumptions that overestimate how happy customers really are. Our research shows that 96% of executives believe customers are willing to recommend their products and services based on past experiences. But in reality, not even half ( 48% ) of customers actually do. Left unaddressed, this gap shows up as weaker referral-driven acquisition, missed cross-sell opportunities, and customers who quietly shop competitors at their next major financial decision, exactly the outcomes banks believe their CX is already delivering. Moving beyond digital convenience to AI-powered value. Now that AI shows up everywhere, from search engines and shopping apps to workplace software, customers are becoming more comfortable with AI agents handling routine banking tasks, especially when those tasks reduce effort without increasing perceived risk. For example, 33% of banking consumers say they may soon let AI agents do things like fill in loan or credit-card applications for them. That creates a practical opening for banks to improve onboarding, servicing, and everyday interactions. 96% of frontline associates in banks plan to expand their use of AI in the next two years, nearly doubling adoption from 47% two years ago. Half of bank executives are already using AI at scale for customer service (chatbots, messaging, self‑service portals). 28% of banking executives say they have enabled agentic AI in some or most CX activities, higher than the cross‑sector average. These figures point to where banks are concentrating automation first: high-volume, low-complexity servicing, such as balance inquiries, card activation, payment status, and application intake. This frees staff for interactions where judgment and reassurance are needed. The future of banking CX will be human-led and AI-powered. As AI adoption accelerates, banking customers will continue to rely on human expertise for complex decisions. As artificial intelligence poses a bigger threat to the banking industry, lenders need to emphasize their human element to maintain customer relationships. That’s according to Udi Ziv, the CEO of Personetics, a fintech that provides banks and credit unions with insights, data analysis and relationship management tools. The human channel “is the biggest moat or the biggest differentiator the banks have” versus large language models and AI agents, Ziv said during an interview at last month’s Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. “The human side of the bank, when it comes to relationships, is extremely important,” and banks are investing in that with more branches and banker hires, he said. Personetics counts half of the top 40 retail banks in North America as customers, Ziv said, including Truist, Huntington and Royal Bank of Canada. KeyBank , for one, uses New York-based Personetics to provide customers with increased transaction detail. With AI tools going from analysis to action, big banks JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citi have blocked AI agent access to customer accounts. Wells Fargo is informing customers of their responsibility when using AI tools. PNC CEO Bill Demchak , for his part, has said agent-only transactions will never happen. Banks face moderate risk from AI-related business disruption over the next five years, largely due to “increased technological competition on processes and products,” Fitch Ratings said Oct. 22. Customers linking their bank accounts to large language models is “an existential threat to the industry,” Ziv said, because it could disintermediate banks’ relationships with customers and turn lenders into “an invisible utility. ”. He pointed to the telecommunications industry, saying companies Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile owned customer relationships until Apple’s iPhone came along. “That's the risk that banks are facing,” Ziv said. “It’s not that they're not going to exist. Banks may cite safety and security reasons to block agents, but fear of losing business is the greater concern, Ziv said. “These very large banks are saying, we're not ready for this,” he said. Customers may want the ability to handle certain bank functions through AI platforms, while preferring direct interaction with the bank for other tasks, he said at Money20/20. Ziv said it’s not “game over” for banks, which have their own competitive moats, he said. Those include breadth and depth of financial data, which LLMs don’t have because banks don't have to give that data away via open banking, and the ability to serve customers in various ways, including human channels such as relationship managers, branches and call centers, he said. Indeed, a JPMorgan Chase billboard in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Oct. 31 advertised, “Money questions. Human answers. ”. “Is AI a threat or an opportunity? I think it's both,” Ziv said. title: Can banks explain every AI agent action to the FCA?
excerpt: Third-party AI agents are knocking on the doors of customer bank accounts just as regulators begin using AI to scrutinise the banks themselves. That leaves lenders with a hard problem. According to Corlytics , they must separate legitimate customer activity from unauthorised actions, and they must be able to show how their controls, decisions and lines of accountability fit together. Picture the scenario. An AI agent attempts to access a customer’s account and the bank blocks it. That single decision raises questions about authorisation, fraud controls and what the customer actually intended. Was the agent a rogue actor, or was it simply carrying out the customer’s instructions?. According to Axios, several major US banks have detected third-party AI agents accessing customer accounts, with some reportedly going beyond what users had asked them to do. A number of these banks are now limiting access while they work out how to distinguish genuine customer activity from behaviour that should be stopped. Regulators are adding another layer of scrutiny. The Financial Times reported that the FCA intends to use AI to automate more of its supervisory and enforcement work. The watchdog already applies AI to documents, emails and interviews, and it wants to extend this across authorisations, supervision and enforcement. Borrowing from Aretha Franklin’s “Who’s Zoomin’ Who?”, the question is who is really watching whom, and who holds control. The customer’s agent looks into the bank, the bank monitors the agent, and the regulator examines the bank. Throughout, the bank is expected to know what happened, explain why and identify who was responsible. Plenty of watching is taking place, but watching is not the same as control. An agent may well be acting for the customer. Yet “the customer authorised it” is not a catch-all answer. Banks need to know what was authorised, for how long, across which accounts and for which actions, and whether the agent could hand instructions to other systems. Simply blocking agents may contain one risk, but it does not resolve how banks will recognise, limit and monitor agents that customers expect to work. The real decisions concern what an agent can see, what it can do, how permission is verified and what evidence is retained. With AI-powered supervision, firms may face faster and broader questions. Banks will need joined-up evidence rather than polished summaries written after the event. If records sit across disconnected systems and teams, a bank may hold all the data yet still fail to tell a coherent story. The likely friction is mundane rather than dramatic. The customer says, “I told it to do that. ” The bank says, “We didn’t know it was doing that. ” The regulator says, “Show us how you knew. ”. Banks that can trace a rule through to the action, the control and the accountable person will have a far stronger answer than “we have an AI policy”. Read the full Corlytics post here. title: US bank regulator issues first-ever AI guidance for examiners
excerpt: New subscriber benefit!. Copied to clipboard. Out of gifts for the month. Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month. Share this article paywall-free. Email. Copy Link. By Pete Schroeder. WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Big bank supervisors should monitor how lenders use artificial intelligence but should not treat it as distinct from other risks, according to new regulatory guidance issued on Wednesday, as authorities globally ramp up their efforts to contain AI-driven risks. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which oversees large national banks, issued what it said was the first-ever guidance for how examiners should probe banks' AI usage, according to a copy of the document seen by Reuters. Under the new framework, first reported by Reuters, the OCC says banks are not expected to establish separate risk parameters for AI use and examiners should not treat the technology as a unique risk. But examiners should consider the way a lender is using AI, as well as the size and complexity of the lender. While the document is not legally binding like a rule, banks typically comply closely with such guidance. Banking regulators worldwide have been querying lenders about their AI use, worried the technology poses major cybersecurity and potentially financial stability risks. In the US, regulators have been asking banks about their use of advanced AI models, what limits banks place on those systems and how they monitor them, Reuters previously reported. The OCC said its examiners should focus on the consequences of potential AI-driven mistakes at banks rather than the sophistication of particular models they're using. For example, it said a simple AI agent that is authorized to initiate transactions could be considered riskier than a sophisticated model deployed for internal purposes. Higher-risk uses of AI may require greater restrictions on autonomy or more direct human oversight, the document said. (Reporting by Pete Schroeder; editing by Michelle Price). Facebook. Twitter. title: JPMorgan Chase warns that AI is outrunning enterprise defenses, and the problem is bigger than cybersecurity
excerpt: JPMorganChase warns that AI is outrunning enterprise defenses, and the problem is bigger than cybersecurity. Artificial Intelligence AI News Security. By Srikanth RP On Nov 4, 2026. 0 10. Share. When JPMorganChase’s global technology leadership team published “200 days into the frontier: What we know and what to do now” on November 2, 2026, it skipped the usual conversation about AI adoption, productivity and innovation. JPMorganChase asks what happens when increasingly capable AI systems change the speed, scale and complexity of enterprise threats. Its central argument is that AI is changing the economics and speed of cyberattacks faster than enterprises are improving their ability to defend themselves. The bank’s framing is deliberately wider than security. It treats the challenge as a question of technology risk, enterprise resilience, infrastructure dependency and corporate governance, which makes it a message for CEOs and boards as much as for CIOs, CISOs and CTOs. The core warning is that vulnerability discovery and attack automation are accelerating while remediation is not keeping pace. Four shifts reshaping the threat landscape JpMorganChase identifies four forces behind that gap. The first is speed: AI is compressing the time it takes to find vulnerabilities and automate attacks, so enterprises can no longer assume that traditional patching and response timelines will hold. The second is autonomy. AI agents are moving beyond answering questions to accessing enterprise systems, retrieving information and executing tasks, and their capabilities can exceed the authority and controls assigned to them. The third is scale. A flaw in a widely deployed technology can force urgent remediation across an entire enterprise, and risks that once looked manageable can become material very quickly. The fourth is dependency. AI growth deepens reliance on semiconductors, data centres, telecommunications, water and electricity, which means digital resilience can no longer be separated from the resilience of physical infrastructure. Technology debt is now a security liability JPMorganChase’s sharpest claim is that technology which still works is not necessarily technology that is safe. It points to unsupported operating systems and programming platforms, outdated open-source libraries, legacy applications that no longer receive patches, ageing network and computing hardware, and internet-facing systems running old software. Its example is PHP, where security fixes for serious vulnerabilities were available only for the current version, leaving organisations on older versions to upgrade or remove the dependency. The practical advice starts with a complete inventory of hardware and software. Each asset should be judged on exposure, meaning whether it can be reached from the internet, on protection, meaning whether it can still receive timely fixes, and on impact, meaning whether its compromise could disrupt customers or critical operations. Any exception to an upgrade should come with an accountable owner, funding, compensating controls and a dated exit plan. In other words, technology debt is no longer just an IT modernisation problem. It is a business risk. Rebuilding the perimeter The bank also separates patching vulnerabilities from reducing the exposure that makes them exploitable. Firewalls, VPN gateways and remote-access tools remain attractive targets precisely because they face the internet, and JPMorganChase cites recent Citrix vulnerabilities as an illustration. Its answer is an independent layer in front of sensitive systems that screens out known attacks and malicious traffic, verifies users through multifactor authentication, and authorises only approved individuals, with the underlying system never directly reachable from the internet. There is a caveat that CIOs will recognise. That protective layer needs its own redundancy and tested fallback arrangements, or it simply becomes the next single point of failure. Capability

CyberCartel, a hacking group with a long history of targeting Latin American businesses, has been using AI agents, including SpaceX's Grok and Anthropic's Claude, to automate attacks on financial institutions such as banks and mobile payment apps. Passwords and customer data have been stolen, while individuals' bank accounts have also been accessed with little input from criminals in the latest example of criminals turning to AI-powered cyberattacks. That research comes from a cybersecurity startup called Straiker, with its findings shared by The Information. While CyberCartel has been an active threat since at least 2012, its new leveraging of the power of AI has leveled up its attacks in recent months. Now, the research shows that the group can attack more businesses at a speed previously not possible when using human-powered hacks. Straiker shared its research with both SpaceX and Anthropic, and both firms are working to lock CyberCartel out of their services. The latter has already been able to block access to Claude. Chinese lab Moonshot AI's agent has also been used by the hacking group, but Straiker is still trying to get in touch with the company. While it's true that AI models normally have protections in place to prevent them from being used to carry out cyberattacks, they've proven surprisingly easy to bypass. In this case, CyberCartel reportedly simply told the models that they were being used in test environments. If one model refused to proceed, the hackers used a different model. If that also refused, the AI agents would be tasked with deploying malware instead. Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware. Watch full video here:. Notably, CyberCartel doesn't appear to be using Anthropic's Mythos for its recent attacks. The company caused a stir earlier this year when it announced the new model, warning that hackers could use it and models like it for attacks like those carried out by CyberCartel. Its release also saw security teams around the globe rush to address thousands of vulnerabilities that the model had identified. This is far from the first time that Anthropic has been faced with the news that its AI is being used by bad actors. The company shared details of its AI being used to carry out a cyberattack in November 2025. Later, Claude was used to break the security of OpenAI , an Anthropic competitor in the AI space. That hack was carried out by researchers rather than criminals, at least. Raiker's research on AI-powered attacks on Latin American financial institutions comes just days after news broke that South Korean authorities are investigating a similar issue affecting local banks. Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Shinhan Bank are among the South Korean banks affected, with at least 25,000 Shinhan Bank customers having their personal credit information leaked. AI companies are well aware of the risks their products pose. Nvidia, the graphics card company that now focuses on producing hardware for AI data centers, recently launched the Open Agent Safety Platform. The software platform and reference system design were developed to secure rogue AI agents via a new hardware and software security stack. It's hoped that it will go some way toward preventing agents from escaping their sandboxes, executing unauthorized code, gaining unauthorized access to critical infrastructure, or bypassing guardrails. Trustworthy AI needs more than a better model. It needs a better system.
excerpt: . As AI moves into the physical world and more consequential decisions, trust will depend on what surrounds the model as much as what happens inside it. The debate around artificial intelligence has been dominated by capability. Models have become larger, faster and more powerful, taking on tasks that would have seemed beyond the reach of software only a few years ago. But capability is only part of the equation. As AI moves from experimentation into real-world deployment, organizations face a harder question: how do you rely on systems whose outputs are inherently probabilistic when the consequences matter?. That challenge runs through a recent New Era of Engineering podcast conversation between Daniela Rus, Director of the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, and Mark Roberts, Head of the Capgemini Global AI Futures Lab and CTO of Applied Sciences at Capgemini Engineering. Their discussion points to an important shift: from asking whether a model can perform a task to asking whether the whole system can be trusted. That matters when AI influences a medical decision, controls a vehicle or robot, or supports a critical business judgment. Competence is essential. But so are predictability and honesty: does the system know what it knows, what it does not know and how confident it should be?. This is where the idea of “AI humility” becomes important. An AI system that admits uncertainty may appear less capable than one that always produces an answer. In practice, it can be more trustworthy. If a model recognizes the limits of its competence, a decision can be escalated, a fallback invoked or a task routed elsewhere. The technology to do this is already emerging. Themis AI, for example, is developing ways to identify uncertainty and errors in AI models and understand what data could improve them. Yet the commercial focus remains heavily weighted toward model performance and capability. The tools for understanding uncertainty may be advancing faster than the appetite to use them. That same shift in thinking applies to safety. Large AI models are probabilistic, so proving that every possible output will always be correct is unrealistic. Assurance therefore has to extend beyond the model itself. Research between MIT and Capgemini is exploring one approach: placing mathematically specified safety layers around learned AI components. The model provides performance and adaptability, while the surrounding layer monitors its proposed actions and keeps the system within defined boundaries. The distinction is important. Many AI “guardrails” still sit within the model itself, effectively relying on the system generating an output to police its own behavior. External assurance provides a different level of control. Commercial aviation offers a useful parallel. People routinely board aircraft heavily dependent on software because decades of engineering, testing, certification, incident analysis and redundancy have created confidence in the wider system. Passengers do not inspect the autopilot or personally verify the pilots. They trust an infrastructure of regulators, engineering processes and accountable organizations to do that for them. AI has yet to develop an equivalent system of trust at the same level of maturity. For organizations, this means moving beyond a narrow focus on model performance. They need to define what acceptable behavior looks like for each application: the accuracy required, the limits that matter, when human intervention is needed and what happens when confidence falls below an agreed threshold. Those decisions also need to be revisited. AI systems change, the data they encounter changes and the environments in which they operate change. Trust cannot be treated as a launch-stage approval. It has to become an ongoing discipline of measurement, monitoring and accountability. That becomes even more important as AI grows more distributed. title: ZAWYA: Jordan: Government signs $4.2mln World Bank grant to advance AI in public services
excerpt: . ZAWYA: Jordan: Government signs $4. 2mln World Bank grant to advance AI in public services. Refinitiv 1 min read. By Staff Writer. AMMAN – The government has signed a $4. 2 million grant agreement with the World Bank to support the development and testing of artificial intelligence applications in public institutions and prepare for the expansion of the Sanad digital platform to include the business sector. The grant forms part of additional financing arrangements for the Youth, Technology and Jobs Project, Al Mamlaka reported, citing World Bank documents. It will fund preparatory activities for the project's additional financing, including the development of practical AI solutions for selected government sectors, studies to identify project components and priorities, and efforts to strengthen the capacity of relevant institutions to design and implement digital solutions. The initiative will focus on developing and testing AI applications to streamline government operations and improve the delivery of public services, according to Al Mamlaka. The applications will include tools capable of carrying out multiple tasks and processes, as well as AI-powered solutions integrated into the Sanad platform. The agreement also provides for the development of a phased plan to expand Sanad's services to business-sector users. This will involve redesigning and simplifying procedures for selected services, testing new digital solutions and preparing the technical specifications required for their implementation. The grant will also support efforts to establish a National Centre of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence, drawing on lessons learnt from AI pilot projects and partnerships developed during their implementation. The proposed centre is expected to bring together expertise, data, research and development to accelerate innovation and strengthen Jordan's technological capabilities. The grant-funded activities are also expected to identify government AI applications with the potential for wider implementation, prepare technical plans for scaling them up and strengthen public institutions' capacity to integrate AI into service delivery. In June, the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship said the Sanad application had continued to record rapid growth, with digital identity activations exceeding 2. 7 million citizens and nearly 400,000 daily active users. The ministry said the figures reflected the application's growing role in citizens' daily lives and their increasing reliance on it to access government services digitally, quickly and conveniently. © Copyright The Jordan Times. title: US Banking Regulator Issues First AI Guidance for Examiners
excerpt: . News. US Banking Regulator Issues First AI Guidance for Examiners. The US banking regulator has issued its first guidance for examining banks' use of artificial intelligence. The framework focuses on potential risks, human supervision and the consequences of AI errors. Written By : Akshita Pidiha. Reviewed By : Vijay Laxmi. Published: 4th Nov, 2026 at 8:30 PM. Updated: 4th Nov, 2026 at 8:30 PM. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released the framework on Wednesday, November 4. It is designed to help examiners evaluate how banks are implementing AI in their everyday business. The guidance advises that examiners should not treat artificial intelligence as a standalone risk category. Banks will not be required to develop separate risk standards for AI applications. “Examiners should be focused on how a bank uses AI in its everyday business,” he said. They have to take into account the size of the bank and the complexity of its business. The OCC wants examiners to pay more attention to the damage that AI errors could cause. A model’s risk level should not be based primarily on the technical features of the model. For example, a simple AI tool that can carry out financial transactions may pose a bigger risk than an advanced system used only for internal work. The framework also suggests tighter restrictions on independent AI operations in higher-risk situations. Banks may need stronger human supervision when their systems can take important decisions or carry out financial activities. Also Read: Barclays Plans 5,000 Job Cuts as AI Reshapes Banking Operations. New Framework Rules. The OCC said the document is not a mandatory regulation for banks. It does not set any new rules that financial institutions must follow. Instead, it offers direction to examiners on how to review the risk management systems banks already have in place. The regulator said, "The OCC expects that bank activities are conducted in a safe and sound manner and consistent with applicable laws and regulations. ". The guidance also applies to smaller community banks. Examiners must consider the size of each bank, its business activities and the risks it faces during their reviews. The move comes as financial regulators in several countries pay closer attention to the growing use of AI in banking. They are studying possible threats linked to cybersecurity, AI systems that operate independently and financial stability. Banks are using AI more often for customer services and other daily activities. Regulators want to make sure these tools are used safely and under proper supervision. title: Äthiopiens Cooperative Bank of Oromia und Kifiya starten KI-gestützte Plattform für Scharia-konforme Finanzierung
excerpt: Äthiopiens Cooperative Bank of Oromia und Kifiya starten KI-gestützte Plattform für Scharia-konforme Finanzierung. Хориж хабарлари 12:45 / 04. 11. 2026. Die Cooperative Bank of Oromia (Coopbank) und das äthiopische Fintech-Unternehmen Kifiya Financial Technology haben „Michu Mizan“ eingeführt, eine KI-gestützte digitale Plattform, die darauf abzielt, den Zugang zu schariakonformen Finanzierungen für unterversorgte Kleinunternehmen zu erweitern. Bereits in der Pilotphase wurden über 200 Millionen Birr an mehr als 4. 000 Kunden vergeben. Die Initiative verbindet die zinsfreien Bankdienstleistungen der Coopbank mit dem Know-how von Kifiya in den Bereichen künstliche Intelligenz, Datenanalyse und digitale Finanzinfrastruktur. Die Einführung bringt zwei Unternehmen zusammen, die in der sich rasch entwickelnden Finanzdienstleistungsbranche des zweitbevölkerungsreichsten Landes Afrikas unterschiedliche, sich jedoch ergänzende Rollen einnehmen. Die Coopbank, die 2004 gegründet wurde und 2005 ihren Betrieb aufnahm, ist aus der Genossenschaftsbewegung des Landes hervorgegangen und bietet sowohl konventionelle als auch zinsfreie Bankdienstleistungen an. Kifiya, ein 2012 gegründetes Fintech-Unternehmen mit Sitz in Addis Abeba, hat sein Geschäft darauf ausgerichtet, mithilfe von Daten und künstlicher Intelligenz Finanzdienstleistungen auf Unternehmen und Privatpersonen auszuweiten, die von herkömmlichen Kreditgebern oft übersehen werden. Michu Mizan wird über das zinsfreie Bankgeschäft der Coopbank betrieben und nutzt künstliche Intelligenz sowie alternative Daten zur Prüfung von Finanzierungsanträgen. Die Plattform bietet vollständig digitale Anträge und Finanzierungsentscheidungen in Echtzeit, ohne dass traditionelle Sicherheiten erforderlich sind. Mit dieser Einführung wird die bestehende Partnerschaft der beiden Institute über „Michu“, ihre digitale Finanzierungsplattform für Kleinst-, Klein- und Mittelunternehmen (KKMU), die bereits 70 Milliarden Birr ausgezahlt hat, erweitert. Michu Mizan erweitert die Zusammenarbeit auf Scharia-konforme Finanzierungen und richtet sich damit an Unternehmen, die Schwierigkeiten beim Zugang zu formellen Finanzmitteln haben oder Produkte benötigen, die mit ihren religiösen Grundsätzen im Einklang stehen. Mehr als 1. 000 Lieferanten haben sich zudem bereits während der Pilotphase Michu Mizan angeschlossen. Durch den Verzicht auf Sicherheiten eröffnet die Plattform Unternehmen den Zugang, die von traditionellen Finanzierungsansätzen nur unzureichend bedient werden. Über „Halal Gebeya“ von Kifiya, einen Scharia-konformen E-Commerce-Dienst, können Kunden im Rahmen des Finanzierungsprozesses Waren bei ihren bevorzugten Anbietern auswählen und kaufen. Auf der gesamten Plattform und in den zugehörigen Lösungen ist die Einhaltung der Scharia von Grund auf integriert, was das Vertrauen der Kunden während des gesamten Finanzierungs- und Kaufprozesses stärkt. „Mizan bedeutet Gleichgewicht, und genau darauf arbeiten wir hin: das wirtschaftliche Potenzial unterversorgter Unternehmen besser mit ihrem Zugang zu angemessener Finanzierung in Einklang zu bringen“, sagte Deribie Asfaw, CEO der Cooperative Bank of Oromia. „Unsere Zusammenarbeit im Rahmen von Michu hat gezeigt, wie wichtig es ist, Finanzdienstleistungen an den tatsächlichen Lebensumständen der Kunden auszurichten. Mit Michu Mizan bauen wir dieses Engagement durch Scharia-konforme digitale Finanzierungen aus, die ihren Glauben respektieren, auf ihre geschäftlichen Bedürfnisse eingehen und wirtschaftliche Wachstumschancen schaffen“, fügte er hinzu. Munir Duri, Gründer und CEO von Kifiya, erklärte, die Plattform wende die KI-basierte Datenentscheidung und die Finanzinfrastruktur des Unternehmens auf Unternehmen an, die in der Vergangenheit Schwierigkeiten hatten, Zugang zu formellen Finanzierungen zu erhalten. „Mit Michu Mizan nutzen wir unsere Erfahrung in der KI-basierten Datenentscheidung und der intelligenten Finanzinfrastruktur, um unterversorgte KKMU sic

The venture holds in-principle approval from the Central Bank of Bahrain and will begin regulated activities only after securing final authorisation. The proposed bank is meant to support institutional clients whose banking needs are regional and international in scope, and Mumtalakat said the venture pairs its long-term investment approach with ARP’s experience in institutional finance and digital financial infrastructure. Target Clients and Operating Design. The bank’s intended clientele spans regulated financial institutions, payment companies, and businesses operating across borders. The partners said the goal is to make banking simpler for clients whose needs extend across multiple markets and currencies, with technology lowering the complexity and cost of serving them. According to the announcement, the bank’s design places artificial intelligence across its operations, with programmable services that connect directly into clients’ systems through APIs. Human oversight, governance, and risk controls would support those services, and products would be rolled out in phases shaped by engagement with prospective clients. The Partners Behind the Venture. Mumtalakat was established on June 29, 2006, under Royal Decree No. 64 of 2006, and is registered with Bahrain’s Ministry of Industry and Commerce as a closed Bahrain Shareholding Company, according to the fund’s corporate governance page. According to the announcement, ARP Digital was co-founded by Yusuf Alireza alongside Abdulla and Abdulaziz Kanoo; ARP Digital describes the brothers on its website as fifth-generation twins from the GCC’s 135-year-old Kanoo Group. ARP Digital is licensed by the Central Bank of Bahrain as a Capital Market-Crypto Assets Service Provider (Cat3), according to ARP Digital’s website , which displays the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) alongside that license. Its product line includes Convert, an institutional over-the-counter digital asset liquidity desk operating around the clock with bilateral settlement in fiat or stablecoin; Send, covering remittance, corridor settlement, and on-ramp and off-ramp flows; and Receive, a collections and payouts product that converts digital assets to fiat for settlement to a client’s bank account. The company says every client is assigned a named relationship manager with direct phone and WhatsApp access, in addition to API and dashboard tools. The company reports more than $3. 5 billion in volume processed, a client base above 450, four or more extended licenses, 4x volume growth in 2025, 99. 99% platform uptime, and support for more than 10 currencies.
